1121.title: Watchfulness
1121.hook: guarding thoughts at the door of the heart
1121.howItsDone: In Orthodox spiritual life, watchfulness is practiced alongside the Jesus Prayer: monks and lay people learn, often with a spiritual father or mother, to notice thoughts early and turn back to prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer of the heart: the mind comes down and stands before God. Your line was the mind in the heart.

A householder is leaving on a long journey. He hands each servant their work, and to one, the porter, he gives a single job: watch the door. That's a short parable in Mark's Gospel. You don't know when the master will be back, Jesus says. Evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning. So stay awake. He's speaking privately to four disciples on the Mount of Olives, and then he widens it past them: "And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch." Yesterday, the heart. Today, the porter who stands at its door. The Orthodox teachers of prayer have a Greek word for his job: nepsis. Watchfulness.

Nepsis is the opposite of drunk. It's being sober, clear, awake. Peter's first letter has the same pair of ideas, in the King James: "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour." Sober and vigilant together. That's watchfulness. The teachers gathered in a collection called the Philokalia make much of it, and one of their pictures is a door. Thoughts come knocking all day long. Plenty are harmless: lunch, the weather, a song. Some aren't: a resentment, a craving, a cutting reply. Watchfulness doesn't mean you'll never have the thought. It means you see it at the door, before you've let it in and given it a chair. Some of these writers trace how a bad thought takes over. First it knocks. Then you start talking with it. Then you agree with it. Then it's running the house. The earlier you notice, the easier the door is to close. Proverbs has the same instinct: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life." Keep, as in guard. Everything that comes out of a life passes through that door first. So yesterday and today belong together. The prayer of the heart brings you home. Watchfulness keeps the house. You can't guard a door you never stand near. And a person at rest in the heart is in a good spot to see who's knocking.

Let your attention settle in your chest again, and watch the door. When a thought comes, don't chase or fight it; name it quietly, planning, worrying, wanting, remembering, and go back to watching, and if you pray, bring the hard ones before God. If a thought of harming yourself knocks, please don't sit alone with it: call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Nepsis. Watchfulness: a sober, wakeful attention that stands at the door of the heart and sees each thought as it comes.
Your line: guard the door. Knocking isn't the same as coming in. See you tomorrow.

1122.title: The gift of tears
1122.hook: holy grief: tears that wash rather than wound
1122.howItsDone: Orthodox teachers speak of the gift of tears as something received, not produced; it is tied to repentance, confession and prayer, and they describe it as leading to joy rather than despair.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nepsis: the porter at the door of the heart, seeing each thought before it comes in. Your line was guard the door.

Peter is sitting by a fire in a courtyard, the night Jesus is arrested. Someone says he was with Jesus. He says he doesn't know the man. It happens again, and again. Then, while he's still speaking, a rooster crows. Luke says the Lord turned, and looked at Peter, and Peter remembers what Jesus told him would happen. The King James says it in seven words: "And Peter went out, and wept bitterly." You met that night back on day sixty-seven. Those tears weren't the end of Peter's story. They were closer to a turning point. The Orthodox teachers of prayer have a word for weeping like that, and they call it a gift.

Penthos is Greek for mourning, grief. Mourning gets a blessing of its own in the Sermon on the Mount: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted." In The Ladder of Divine Ascent, a monk called John Climacus gives a whole step to mourning, and gives it a strange name: joy-making mourning. Grief with joy folded inside it. Penthos isn't despair. Despair looks at what's broken, a harsh word, a wasted year, a friend let down, and says it's hopeless. Penthos grieves the very same thing in the presence of God. One closes a door; the other opens one. The Psalms know the difference: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy." Another psalm asks God to keep them: "put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?" Not one wasted. That's why the teachers call tears a gift, not a skill. You can't manufacture them, and nobody is asked to. They come or they don't, and grief can be dry-eyed too: a quiet ache, a softening heart. And it isn't only about sin. At the tomb of his friend Lazarus, John's Gospel says it in two words: "Jesus wept." Tears that wound leave a person smaller, ashamed and alone. Tears that wash leave them lighter, turned back toward God and toward the people they love.

Bring to mind one thing you're sorry for, or one loss you've never stopped to grieve, and stay with it without pushing it away or pushing yourself to cry; if tears come, let them, and if they don't, a soft ache counts too. If you pray, hold it out to God; if not, simply stay with it kindly. And if the grief ever turns into not wanting to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Penthos. Holy grief: mourning that softens rather than crushes, the tears the Orthodox teachers call a gift.
Your line: tears that wash. Grief, held before God, can open a door. Until tomorrow.

1123.title: The prayer rope
1123.hook: a knotted wool rope, one Jesus Prayer per knot
1123.howItsDone: Orthodox monks and lay people pray the Jesus Prayer on a knotted wool rope, moving the thumb one knot for each prayer; in Greek it is called a komboskini, in Russian chotki.

segments.voice: Yesterday, penthos: holy grief, tears that wash rather than wound. Your line was tears that wash.

A loop of black wool sits in a monk's hand. It isn't a string of beads. It's knots, each one tied by hand, close together, with a small woolen cross where the loop closes. His thumb finds a knot, and he says a short prayer. Then the next knot, another prayer. Nothing about it is fancy. It would fit in a coat pocket. You met the Jesus Prayer back on day ninety-nine; this is the thing in the hand that keeps it company. In Greek it's called a komboskini. In Russian it's chotki, and that's today's word.

Why knots at all? Paul tells the Thessalonians, in three words, "Pray without ceasing." For anyone who takes that at its word, a rope helps: a way to keep going without losing your place, or your attention. It's cheap, quiet and always to hand. There's a story about the knots. Tradition says a monk tied knots in a cord to count his prayers, and the devil kept coming in the night and untying them. So he was shown a new kind of knot, woven out of little crosses, that the devil couldn't undo. It's a legend, but it says plainly what the rope is for: a prayer, tied tight. The prayer itself is short. Its usual form asks the Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, to have mercy on me, a sinner, and its words echo the Gospels. A blind man by the road at Jericho shouts, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." A tax collector in the temple won't even lift his eyes, and prays, "God be merciful to me a sinner." Put those two together and you can hear it. And the rope isn't a scoreboard. In this tradition the point is attention, not the total. The knot under the thumb brings a wandering mind back, gently, the way a friend's hand on your shoulder does. Lose your place, and you simply carry on from the next knot.

Tie a few knots, slowly, in whatever is at hand: a shoelace, a thread, a phone charger if that's all you've got. Hold it and let your thumb find one knot at a time; if you pray, say the Jesus Prayer once for each, and if you don't, take one breath for each, a single moment of attention. When your mind wanders, the next knot calls you back.
Chotki. The Orthodox prayer rope: knotted wool, one Jesus Prayer for each knot, and a thumb that keeps the place.
Your line: a knot, a prayer. The rope is for attention, not for counting. Go gently.

1124.title: The elder
1124.hook: Orthodox Christians seek a spiritual father or mother for guidance
1124.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians seek guidance from a spiritual father or mother, who may be the priest who hears their confession; some travel to monasteries to ask a recognized elder for a word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chotki: a rope of wool, a prayer at every knot. Your line was a knot, a prayer.

Night, in the temple of the Lord. A boy named Samuel, who serves there, hears his name called and runs to the old priest Eli. Here I am, he says. Eli says, I didn't call you. Go back and lie down. It happens again, and again. Eli is old, his eyes growing dim, but he's the one who works out what's going on: the Lord is calling the boy. So he tells Samuel what to say if it comes once more: "Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth." Eli doesn't hear the voice himself. He helps someone else hear it. That's the picture behind today's word, from the Russian Orthodox tradition: starets. The elder.

Starets, in Russian, simply means an old man, but the role isn't really about age. An elder is a monk, sometimes a nun, now and then a lay person, known for prayer and for seeing clearly into hearts, whom others seek out for guidance. A woman in the role is a staritsa; in Greek the elder is a geron. Tradition traces the role back to the desert, where people walked out to an old monk's cell and said, in substance, Abba, give me a word. Not a lecture: one sentence to live on for a while. Abba means father; a woman teacher was called amma, mother. Why need this? Because watchfulness, tears and the prayer rope can all be bent by the one doing them. A mind can mistake its own pride for holiness, and never notice. Proverbs puts it plainly: "Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety." The elder is a second pair of eyes on the soul. Dostoevsky put an elder at the heart of The Brothers Karamazov, Father Zosima, and described the bond as freely handing your will to someone wiser, for the sake of becoming free. That's the strong form: a long, trusted relationship, not advice on demand. In everyday Orthodox life, this guidance can come through a priest who hears confession and becomes a spiritual father. Other churches use other names: Catholics speak of spiritual direction, and some Protestants of a mentor or a pastor.

Let one question rise, something you've been deciding on your own, and then let a face come to mind: someone you trust who sees more clearly than you on this, a grandparent, a pastor, an old friend, a teacher. Imagine asking them, and wonder what they might see that you can't. If you pray, you can say Samuel's line: Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth.
Starets. The elder: someone seasoned in prayer whom others seek out for guidance, a second pair of eyes on the soul.
Your line: go to the elder. Nobody has to see their own soul alone. Until tomorrow.

1125.title: Mount Athos
1125.hook: a peninsula of monasteries given over to prayer
1125.howItsDone: Orthodox monks on Mount Athos keep a daily round of services, private prayer and work, with long vigils before feasts; Orthodox Christians and other visitors go there on pilgrimage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the starets: the elder who helps another person hear. Your line was go to the elder.

Knock. Knock. Knock-knock. Well before sunrise, a monk walks slowly around a stone courtyard carrying a long wooden board, striking it with a mallet, a rhythm that carries over the walls and down the cliffs to the sea. It's the call to prayer. This is Mount Athos, a mountain at the tip of a long finger of land in northern Greece, given over to monasteries. Watchfulness, the prayer rope and the Jesus Prayer are daily work here. Today's word: Mount Athos.

The monks call it the Holy Mountain, in Greek Hagion Oros: a whole peninsula of monasteries, small monastic villages, and hermits' huts clinging to the rocks above the water. There's a story the monks tell about how it began. Tradition says Mary, the mother of Jesus, was at sea when a storm drove her ship off course; she came ashore here, loved the place, and asked her Son to give it to her. So Athos is called the Garden of the Mother of God, and the monks speak of her as its abbess, its true head. Why a mountain? Luke gives one picture of Jesus at prayer: "he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God." The monks take that night of prayer as a pattern. Before great feasts they keep vigils that run through the night, with candles, chant, and the lamps before the icons set gently swinging as the feast comes to its height. And here's the part worth carrying home. The monks don't describe themselves as escaping the world. They speak of praying for it: for people who never pray, for people who will never learn their names, for the whole world. So somewhere on a cliff above the sea, someone may be praying for you, and will never meet you. The psalmist looked at the hills, asked where help comes from, and answered himself: "My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth."

segments.voice: Close your eyes and picture it: stone walls on a cliff, a wooden board knocking, lamps lit in a dark church, and below, the sea going from black to gray to silver. Stand quietly at the back; you don't have to say anything. If you pray, join their prayer for the world by naming one person far away from you; if you don't, simply hold that person in mind while the light comes up.
Mount Athos. The Holy Mountain: a peninsula of monasteries in Greece, given over to prayer for the world.
Your line: the holy mountain. On a cliff above the sea, the world is being prayed for. That's today, done.

1126.title: Lay aside all earthly cares
1126.hook: in the Cherubic hymn of the Liturgy, the people join the angels
1126.howItsDone: In the Orthodox Divine Liturgy the choir sings the Cherubic Hymn while the clergy carry the bread and wine in procession, the Great Entrance; the people stand, and some cross themselves and bow as the gifts pass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mount Athos: monks on a cliff, praying for the world. Your line was the holy mountain.

Partway through the Orthodox Divine Liturgy, the singing slows right down. The choir begins a hymn so drawn out that a single word can take a long breath to sing. A door in the screen of icons opens. The clergy come out carrying the bread and wine for communion, walk them through the church with candles and incense, then back through the central doors to the altar. And the words the choir is singing ask everyone standing there to do something hard. Put it all down. Not later. Now. Today's word is the hymn's own phrase: lay aside all earthly cares.

It's called the Cherubic Hymn. In substance it says: we who, in a mystery, represent the cherubim, and sing the thrice-holy hymn to the life-giving Trinity, let us now lay aside all earthly cares, so that we may receive the King of all, escorted unseen by the hosts of angels. Alleluia. Look at what that claims. The people in the room, tired, distracted, holding coats and children, stand for the cherubim, angels the Bible places close to God. The thrice-holy hymn is the song Isaiah heard the seraphim crying to one another in his vision: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." The Greek word for care in the hymn is merimna: worry, the pull of a divided mind. The Bible knows that pull. In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus says, "Take therefore no thought for the morrow." And Peter's first letter says, "Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you." None of these says your cares don't matter. Peter says where to throw them. The hymn says to lay them aside for now, like a bag set down at a door, so you can be fully in the room. They'll still be there when the service ends. But for a few minutes, they won't be running it.
screen: `A BAG SET DOWN AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees, name the care that's heaviest right now, just one, and feel its weight for a breath, as if it were in your hands. Then slowly set it down beside you, like a bag on the floor by a door; it isn't gone, and you can pick it up after. If you pray, hand it over with Peter's line, casting all your care upon him; if you don't, simply sit with empty hands.
Lay aside all earthly cares. The line from the Cherubic Hymn that asks the people to set their worries down and sing with the angels.

1127.title: Heaven on earth
1127.hook: the Orthodox see the Divine Liturgy as joining heaven's worship now
1127.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians gather for the Divine Liturgy on Sundays and feasts; with icons, incense and chant, the service is understood as a sharing in the worship of heaven, and it leads to communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Cherubic Hymn, and cares set down at the door. Your line was lay aside all cares.

An old Russian chronicle tells of envoys sent by a prince of Kiev to Constantinople. They're led into the great church there while the Liturgy is being sung: chant, lamps, incense, a dome overhead. Back home, they struggle to describe it. The chronicle gives their report, in substance: we didn't know whether we were in heaven or on earth. We only know that God dwells there among people, and we can't forget that beauty. You heard the envoys' story back on day eight hundred five. Whatever historians make of it, it's a striking thing to say about a church service. It's the last stop on the Orthodox way of the heart.

For Orthodox Christians, that line isn't only a traveler's compliment. It's close to how their church describes the Divine Liturgy itself. Not a play about heaven, not a memory of heaven, but a joining in, now, with worship already going on there. The Bible gives them the picture. In Revelation, John is shown the throne of God, and creatures around it who "rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come." A song with no gaps in it. The Liturgy steps into that song for a while. The letter to the Hebrews tells ordinary believers: "ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels." Ye are come. Not someday. The building says it too. The saints on the icons stand with the people, so the room is never only as full as it looks. Incense goes up, and Revelation has that picture as well: the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rising before God. That's why yesterday's hymn asked everyone to lay their cares aside: they're about to stand in a crowded room. Look back across this week: guarding the door of the heart, tears that wash, a knot for each prayer, an elder to help you hear, a mountain at prayer, cares set down. It all leads here, to the plain claim the Orthodox make about their worship: heaven is not far off. It's near.

Let the room around you grow larger in your mind: not empty, but full. If you pray, say the line from Revelation, holy, holy, holy, and let it join a song the text says never stops. If you don't, simply sit as if you were in very good company, unhurried, unseen, and not alone.
Heaven on earth. The Orthodox picture of the Divine Liturgy: not watching heaven from far away, but joining its worship now.
Your line: heaven is near. Tomorrow, a new room in the house: Francis of Assisi.

chat.says: Why are Orthodox services so long and so full of candles and chant? Is it a show?
options: They see the Liturgy as joining heaven's worship now, a song already going, not a show.
It's mostly about keeping old customs alive; the beauty matters more than prayer.
It's a reward for the holiest believers, the only ones who get to feel heaven there.
chat.meaning: For the Orthodox, the Divine Liturgy isn't a play or a memory of heaven but a joining in, now, with worship already going on there. Heaven is near.
